title: Auditing Machine Unlearning: A Systematic Research on Whether Models Truly Forget

paper.title: Auditing Machine Unlearning: A Systematic Research on Whether Models Truly Forget
paper.abstract:
Abstract Machine unlearning has been extensively studied in response to growing privacy concerns and regulatory requirements. However, auditing whether unlearning algorithms have truly erased the influence of specific data remains an open challenge. The lack of reliable and practical auditing mechanisms can lead to critical privacy risks, such as residual information leakage.
This paper initiates a systematic investigation into whether existing unlearning algorithms can truly forget the designated data. We propose the first practical and general-purpose auditing framework for machine unlearning, inspired by the concept of proof of ignorance. Our framework addresses the key practicality limitations of existing methods by eliminating the need for retraining-from-scratch baselines, avoiding the training of large numbers of shadow models, and requiring no intrusive intervention in the original training process.
To evaluate the effectiveness of our framework, we first conduct validation experiments to verify its soundness and completeness. We then perform comprehensive experiments across six datasets and ten representative unlearning methods. The results demonstrate that our framework reliably distinguishes between successful and failed unlearning. In particular, we observe that retraining-based and fine-tuning-based methods can achieve effective unlearning, even when the target data remain in the original dataset. In contrast, de-optimization-based methods fail to achieve true unlearning and instead degrade the model’s performance. Fisher/Hessian-based methods also fail to unlearn requested data, even formal certification is provided.
Moreover, we show that our framework is robust against fake unlearning attempts and generalizes well to large language models.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Machine unlearning has emerged as a critical paradigm for enabling data deletion in machine learning models, particularly in response to growing concerns around user privacy and regulatory requirements such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [ 1 ] . The goal of unlearning is to ensure that a trained model forgets specific data samples upon request, such that the resulting model behaves as if the data had never been used in training [ 2 , 3 ] . Motivated by this objective, a wide range of unlearning algorithms has been proposed [ 4 , 5 ] . However, the problem of auditing unlearning outcomes remains largely underexplored. In most existing studies, outcome auditing is treated as a peripheral issue or mentioned only briefly, without a systematic investigation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Auditing machine unlearning is critical. Its goal is to determine whether the unlearned model has truly forgotten the knowledge associated with the data requested for removal. An effective audit not only reassures data owners who exercise their right to revoke personal data, but also certifies the correctness and reliability of unlearning algorithms. Straightforward auditing approaches include parametric auditing and behavioral auditing [ 6 , 8 ] . Parametric auditing evaluates whether the parameters of the unlearned model remain within a bounded distance from those of a model retrained from scratch without the unlearning data. In contrast, behavioral auditing assesses if the unlearned model exhibits similar behavior to that of the retrained model when evaluated on specific datasets. Despite their conceptual soundness, both approaches share a fundamental limitation: they require access to a retrained model that excludes the unlearning data. This renders them impractical for two reasons. First, retraining a model from scratch incurs substantial computational overhead. Second, if one already possesses the retrained model, auditing becomes unnecessary, as this retrained model can be directly deployed as the unlearned model. Another line of research on unlearning auditing is based on membership inference [ 9 , 10 ] , which aims to determine whether the unlearned data still belong to the training set of the unlearned model. However, membership inference typically requires training a large number of shadow models, resulting in heavy computational cost [ 11 ] . Moreover, it often suffers from limited inference accuracy and yields only probabilistic outcomes without explicit accuracy guarantees [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Other less mainstream auditing methods rely on backdoors, but they require the unrealistic step of injecting backdoors into the training data before model training [ 15 ] . An orthogonal research direction focuses on auditing unlearning procedures [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] , with the goal of verifying whether mutually agreed unlearning algorithms are executed correctly. In contrast, our work audits unlearning outcomes rather than procedures. This distinction is important because, as we show in the experiments, some unlearning algorithms fail to truly remove the influence of the unlearning data even if they are executed correctly. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a practical and general unlearning auditing framework by addressing three challenges . First , the absence of access to retrained reference models necessitates a self-contained auditing mechanism that does not rely on expensive retraining from scratch. Second , achieving a balance between auditing effectiveness and computational efficiency complicates the design: the auditing method must deliver reliable assessments while incurring significantly lower computational cost than full retraining. Third , there is no definitive ground truth for evaluating whether a given unlearning algorithm, apart from retraining from scratch, has truly achieved the unlearning objective. To address the first and second challenges, our auditing framework constructs verification models by training on only 15 % 15\% of the remaining data, on average, for each verification model. As our verification model is trained on data disjoint from the unlearning set, it provides a valid comparator for evaluating whether the unlearned model has successfully forgotten the targeted data, thus addressing the first challenge. This comparison is grounded in the concept of proof of ignorance. If a verification model, believed to lack knowledge of the unlearning set, can be transformed into the unlearned model through a polynomial-time process, such as updating it with additional data, then the unlearned model is also considered to be ignorant of the same knowledge. Thus, if the unlearned model exhibits behavior closely aligned with that of the verification model or its transformed version, it provides strong evidence that the unlearned model no longer retains the forgotten data. Moreover, although only a subset of the remaining data is used, our framework leverages the insight that a small but representative subset can still capture the distributional characteristics of the original data [ 19 ] , thus addressing the second challenge by striking a balance between computational efficiency and auditing accuracy. To address the third challenge, the lack of ground truth for successful unlearning, we first validate our framework before using it to audit unlearning methods. Then, we use backdoor-based and membership inference-based auditing, along with t-SNE [ 20 ] visualization, as supporting evidence. In summary, this paper makes three contributions . • We initiate a systematical study to examine whether existing popular unlearning algorithms can truly forget the revoked data. To achieve this, we propose the first practical and general auditing framework, grounded in the concept of proof of ignorance. Before applying the framework, we rigorously evaluate its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and validation experiments. • We perform a comprehensive empirical study that evaluates ten unlearning approaches across six datasets, including both image and text domains. We also assess our framework against fake unlearning attempts and demonstrate its effectiveness in successfully detecting them. • We further demonstrate the strong generalizability of our framework by extending the auditing study to large language model (LLM) unlearning scenarios.

Given a learning algorithm A : 𝒟 → ℳ A:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} , where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denotes the data space and ℳ \mathcal{M} represents the model space, a model M M can be trained using A A on a dataset D D , i.e., M = A ⁡ ( D ) M=A(D) . However, this retraining-from-scratch method is computationally intensive. Let U : ℳ × 𝒟 × 𝒟 → ℳ U:\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{D}\times\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} be an unlearning algorithm. An unlearned model M u M_{u} is obtained by applying U U to M M , D D , and D u D_{u} , i.e., M u = U ⁡ ( M , D , D u ) M_{u}=U(M,D,D_{u}) . Ideally, U U is more computationally efficient than retraining from scratch, and the difference between M u M_{u} and M u ∗ M^{*}_{u} is minimized. This difference can be quantified in either the model parameter space [ 21 , 22 ] or the model output space [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Proof of Ignorance. In the proof of ignorance [ 26 , 27 ] , given an instance q q of a complex problem, the prover must demonstrate to the auditor that they do not know the solution s s for the problem q q . To address this, the prover identifies a well-known complex instance q ′ q^{\prime} , with a solution s ′ s^{\prime} that is computationally related to s s , namely, there exists a polynomial-time process that transforms s ′ s^{\prime} to s s . As q ′ q^{\prime} is both well-known and complex, claiming ignorance of its solution s ′ s^{\prime} is considered trustworthy by the auditor. Moreover, since s ′ s^{\prime} is computationally related to s s , ignorance of s ′ s^{\prime} implies ignorance of s s . Threat Model. The model provider employs an unlearning algorithm U U to remove the influence of the requested data D u D_{u} , as specified by the data owner, resulting in an unlearned model M u M_{u} . The model provider, acting as the prover , then aims to validate that the unlearned model M u M_{u} no longer contains information related to D u D_{u} . This validation can be presented either to the data owner or to a trusted third party, such as a regulator, who acts as the auditor . The prover has full access to the original model M M and the training data D D , and can freely modify M M or utilize D D as needed. In contrast, the auditor does not have access to the internal parameters of M M or its variants but can query these models and observe their outputs. The auditor holds the authority to define and enforce the auditing protocol. In particular, the auditor can specify which portions of the data D D are used during the auditing process without accessing the actual data content, and the prover follows these auditing instructions throughout the protocol. This assumption is reasonable, as our objective is to audit the efficacy of unlearning algorithms rather than the honesty of the prover. We will relax this assumption in the experiments by considering scenarios in which the prover performs fake unlearning. This asymmetry of access reflects real-world scenarios where the model provider (the prover) is an ML service platform, while the auditor is a data owner or regulatory authority with limited insight into the internal workings of the model. The assumption that the auditor cannot see the raw data in D D , but can still reference its structure (e.g., via hashes), is reasonable. It reflects the common setting in privacy-preserving audits [ 28 ] , where the auditor must operate under a black-box model due to data sensitivity. Problem Statement. sections.text: Rationale. According to the proof of ignorance, the prover can generate another model M v M_{v} that is guaranteed to exclude the data D u D_{u} . If the prover can then demonstrate that M v M_{v} can be transformed into M u M_{u} through a polynomial-time process, such as further updating M v M_{v} with additional data from D r D_{r} , it becomes credible to assert that M u M_{u} does not contain information from D u D_{u} . Detailed theoretical analyses of our auditing framework are provided in Section IV . Fig. 1: Overview of our auditing framework. The auditor first conducts a preliminary check by comparing outputs from the unlearned model M u M_{u} and the pre-unlearning model M M . If their behavior is highly consistent, unlearning is immediately considered failed. Otherwise, the auditor proceeds to the main protocol: Step 1, the prover trains a verification model M v M_{v} ; Step 2, the auditor compares outputs between M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} ; Step 3, if inconsistent, M v M_{v} is updated or retrained and compared again. If consistency is achieved, unlearning is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected. Overview. As shown in Figure 1 , before initiating the formal auditing process, we conduct a preliminary check: if the unlearned model exhibits behavior nearly identical to the pre-unlearning model, for example, both achieving high accuracy on the unlearning set, it can be immediately flagged as a failure of unlearning. This is because a truly unlearned model is expected to undergo a noticeable behavioral shift, particularly in its performance on the unlearning data. Once such obvious failures are filtered out, we proceed with the main auditing protocol, which consists of three steps . First , the auditor randomly identifies a subset of data D v D_{v} from the remaining data D r = D − D u D_{r}=D-D_{u} , and instructs the prover to use D v D_{v} as a verification set to train a new model M v M_{v} for auditing. Since D v D_{v} is entirely disjoint from D u D_{u} , it is guaranteed that M v M_{v} does not contain any information from D u D_{u} . Second , the auditor compares the outputs of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} . If the outputs of the two models are consistent, it can be trusted that M u M_{u} also does not contain the information of D u D_{u} . This is because consistent outputs indicate that M u M_{u} and M v M_{v} exhibit similar decision boundaries on D u D_{u} . As M v M_{v} is independent of D u D_{u} , such consistence implies that M u M_{u} ’s behavior does not rely on specific features derived from D u D_{u} . However, if the outputs of the two models are inconsistent, the audit proceeds to the third step. In the third step, based on the observed differences in outputs between M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} , the prover decides whether to increase the size of D v D_{v} by adding more data from D r D_{r} or to reduce the size of D v D_{v} by removing some data. If the decision is to increase the size of D v D_{v} , the prover fine-tunes M v M_{v} using the additional data. If the decision is to reduce the size of D v D_{v} , the prover retrains M v M_{v} using the reduced subset. After refining M v M_{v} , the auditor compares the outputs of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} again. If the outputs are consistent, the prover can claim that M u M_{u} does not contain the information of D u D_{u} . If the outputs remain inconsistent, the prover fails to prove ignorance of the presence of D u D_{u} in M u M_{u} . The auditor grants the prover only a single opportunity to refine M v M_{v} for auditing. We will show in Section IV that this single refinement is sufficient to ensure correctness. Each step of our method is elaborated in detail. Step 1. Verification Model Construction. The auditor randomly selects a subset of data from D r D_{r} to form a new dataset D v D_{v} . This selection can be implemented using various randomized sampling techniques to ensure that D v D_{v} is representative of the overall distribution of D r D_{r} while remaining entirely disjoint from D u D_{u} . One straightforward approach is uniform random sampling, where each data point in D r D_{r} has an equal probability of being included in D v D_{v} . This method ensures that the selection process is unbiased and does not favor any particular subset of data. Alternatively, the auditor can use stratified random sampling, where the data points are grouped based on their class labels. Samples are then drawn randomly from each group in proportion to their representation in D r D_{r} . This technique ensures that D v D_{v} retains a distribution similar to that of D r D_{r} , making the auditing process more robust against imbalances in the dataset. sections.heading: IV Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: We first analyze the soundness of the preliminary check and then establish a theoretical connection between the auditing process and the concept of proof of ignorance. Specifically, the instance q q corresponds to the unlearned model M u M_{u} , and the solution s s represents its parameters. Likewise, the instance q ′ q^{\prime} is mapped to the verification model M v M_{v} , and the solution s ′ s^{\prime} to its parameters. Under this mapping, we demonstrate that (1) refining M v M_{v} with additional data is a polynomial-time process; (2) if M v M_{v} can be transformed into M u M_{u} through such refinement, then M u M_{u} can be regarded as having successfully unlearned the target data D u D_{u} ; and (3) a single refinement iteration is sufficient to reach alignment under our framework. sections.heading: V Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and Model Architectures. We use three image datasets: CIFAR10 [ 29 ] , SVHN [ 30 ] , and SkinCancer [ 31 ] , and three text datasets: BBCNews [ 32 ] , AGNews [ 33 ] , and IMDB [ 34 ] , covering both multi-class and binary classification tasks, to evaluate the multi-modal applicability of the proposed auditing framework. For image datasets, the model architecture consists of four CNN blocks followed by three fully connected layers. For text datasets, the model includes an embedding layer, three CNN blocks, and a fully connected layer. Unlearning Methods. We evaluate four representative unlearning methods, along with six of their variants, including Retrain , Adversarial retrain [ 7 ] , Fine-tuning (FT) [ 17 ] , Relabeling [ 22 ] , Relabeling with fine-tuning (Relabel+FT) [ 22 ] , Gradient ascent (GA) [ 35 ] , Gradient ascent with fine-tuning (GA+FT) [ 35 ] , Fisher forgetting [ 36 ] , Hessian forgetting [ 36 , 37 ] , and Certified Hessian forgetting [ 16 ] . Detailed descriptions of these unlearning approaches and datasets are provided in the Appendix. Evaluation Metrics. Since our auditing method relies primarily on model outputs, the evaluation metrics are centered around comparing the outputs of different models. • Model agreement. This metric, defined in Eq. 1 , quantifies the consistency between the outputs of two models. It is calculated as the ratio of the number of data points for which both models produce identical outputs to the total number of data points in the given dataset. This metric is widely used in the literature to evaluate model similarity. • Average Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL). This metric complements the model agreement by measuring the average KL divergence between the output probability distributions of two models across a given dataset. Baselines. We adopt widely recognized auditing methods as baselines [ 4 , 7 ] . • Model Accuracy on the Unlearning Data. This is a straightforward auditing method. The intuition is that if the unlearning data have been properly forgotten, the unlearned model should perform on them similarly to how it performs on the test data. • Membership Inference. This method determines whether a given data sample was in the training set of a target model. If the model has truly forgotten the unlearning data, a membership inference attack should identify them as non-training data. We employ the state of the art technique proposed in [ 9 ] . • Backdoor-based Auditing. This method leverages the principle behind backdoor attacks, where specific data are intentionally misclassified into targeted labels. When the unlearning data are backdoored, a successful unlearning process should eliminate their influence, meaning that the model should no longer misclassify these samples into the targeted labels. For a fair comparison, we adopt the same backdoor attack method used in [ 7 ] .

sections.heading: VI Validation and Ablation Study
sections.text: Before presenting the auditing results on existing unlearning methods, we first validate our auditing framework. The validation focuses on two aspects: soundness and completeness . For soundness, we require that every model accepted by our framework as successfully unlearned indeed no longer retains any knowledge of the unlearning data. For completeness, we require that every model that has truly unlearned the target data is not incorrectly rejected by our framework. Empirically, soundness is evaluated through the false positive rate ( FPR ), while completeness is measured by the false negative rate ( FNR ). Specifically, to assess soundness, we train 100 partially unlearned models, each on a mixed dataset containing 40 % ∼ 60 % 40\%\sim 60\% of D r D_{r} and 40 % ∼ 60 % 40\%\sim 60\% of D u D_{u} . To assess completeness, we train 100 truly unlearned models, each constructed using a randomly selected 60 % ∼ 80 % 60\%\sim 80\% subset of D r D_{r} . The exact sampling ratio is uniformly drawn from the interval [ a % , b % ] [a\%,b\%] . The corresponding results are summarized in Table II . The results show that the auditing framework achieves exceptionally low FPR and FNR values, both below 0.02 0.02 across all six datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness. According to our proposed auditing framework, unlearning approaches based on retraining or fine-tuning, such as Retrain, Adversarial Retrain, Fine-tune, Relabel with Fine-tune, and Gradient Ascent with Fine-tune, successfully achieve the unlearning objective. This is evidenced by the fact that the agreement and KL divergence between the corresponding unlearned models and the verification model are nearly identical to the base agreement and base KL divergence, which serve as reference benchmarks for ideal unlearning behavior. For example, in Table V , the five retraining/fine-tuning-based methods exhibit behavior distinct from the pre-unlearning model, especially on the unlearning dataset D u D_{u} . Specifically, their accuracies on D u D_{u} are 69.15 69.15 for Retrain, 73.87 73.87 for Adversarial Retrain, 76.13 76.13 for Fine-tune, 73.67 73.67 for Relabel with Fine-tune, and 73.40 73.40 for Gradient Ascent with Fine-tune, significantly lower than the pre-unlearning model’s accuracy of 95.92 95.92 on the same data. Following the three-step main auditing protocol, the final agreement rates between the unlearned model M u M_{u} and the verification model M v M_{v} for these methods all exceed the base agreement threshold of 70.30 70.30 . Specifically, the agreement rates are 71.23 71.23 for Retrain, 71.10 71.10 for Adversarial Retrain, 70.53 70.53 for Fine-tune, 70.94 70.94 for Relabel with Fine-tune, and 70.33 70.33 for Gradient Ascent with Fine-tune. Therefore, these methods are deemed to have achieved successful unlearning. This auditing outcome can be further attributed to the nature of these methods. By either retraining the model from scratch or performing targeted fine-tuning on the remaining data, they effectively eliminate the influence of the unlearning data. Thus, the decision boundaries of the unlearned models align closely with those of the verification model. We pay particular attention to the Fine-tune approach, which directly fine-tunes the model on the remaining data without explicitly interacting with or removing the unlearning data. At first glance, this method may appear inadequate from an algorithmic standpoint, as it continues training a model that initially retains knowledge of the unlearning data. However, our auditing results suggest that this approach can indeed achieve the unlearning objective. The underlying reason lies in the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, where continued training on new data causes a model to lose previously acquired knowledge. By exclusively fine-tuning on the remaining data, this forgetting effect is concentrated on the unlearning data, erasing its influence from the model. Another approach that warrants close attention is Adversarial Retrain. Although this method is described as “adversarial” in [ 7 ] , our auditing results suggest that it effectively achieves the unlearning objective. The key mechanism is that it intentionally avoids using the unlearning data during retraining. Instead, it replaces each unlearning sample with a feature-similar sample selected from the remaining dataset. We argue that this substitution strategy constitutes a valid unlearning mechanism. First, it strictly adheres to the unlearning requirement, as the actual unlearning data are excluded from the retraining process. Second, the use of feature-similar data does not violate the privacy or intent of data revocation. These substitute samples are drawn from the remaining, non-revoked data, and therefore do not reintroduce any personal information that the data owner has requested to remove. These methods attempt to “unlearn” by deliberately corrupting the model’s performance on the unlearning data, typically through perturbing the decision boundaries or reversing the gradients associated with those samples. The fundamental flaw in these approaches is their reliance on performance deterioration as a proxy for forgetting. However, poor performance on the unlearning data does not guarantee that the model no longer retains knowledge of those data. In fact, a well-generalized model can perform well even on unseen data that shares the same distribution. Our auditing results support this argument. The models produced by these de-optimization-based approaches exhibit low agreement with verification models. For instance, in Table V , the agreement rates for Relabel and Gradient Ascent are only 30.90 30.90 and 35.17 35.17 , respectively, substantially below the base agreement threshold of 70.30 70.30 . The Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian Forgetting methods also fail to achieve the true objective of unlearning. Fisher Forgetting and Certified Hessian Forgetting can be rejected at an early stage by the preliminary check, as the resulting unlearned models exhibit behavior that is nearly indistinguishable from that of the pre-unlearning model. For instance, in Table V , the accuracy of the Fisher-based unlearned model on the unlearning set D u D_{u} , the remaining set D r D_{r} , and the test set D t D_{t} is 95.87 95.87 , 95.45 95.45 , and 71.62 71.62 , respectively, closely matching the pre-unlearning model’s accuracy of 95.92 95.92 , 95.61 95.61 , and 71.79 71.79 . In contrast, Hessian Forgetting can be readily filtered out by the preliminary check on the image datasets (Tables V , VI , and VII ), but it passes the preliminary check on the text datasets (Tables VIII , IX , and X ) as its accuracy on the unlearning data is substantially reduced. However, this reduction in accuracy is accompanied by a similarly significant drop in agreement with the verification model, and it is therefore still easily identified as a failed unlearning method by the subsequent auditing steps. The underlying reason lies in the design of these approaches. They attempt to remove the influence of the unlearning data through local parameter perturbations derived from second-order approximations of the loss landscape, such as the Fisher information matrix or the Hessian matrix. However, such perturbations are often too limited to induce the behavioral shift required for true unlearning. In some cases, they merely preserve the original model behavior, causing the resulting model to remain highly similar to the pre-unlearning model. In other cases, they degrade model accuracy without genuinely removing the influence of the unlearning data. We pay particular attention to the Certified Hessian unlearning method, as it fails to achieve effective unlearning despite being formally certified. Specifically, the certification refers to satisfying the ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -unlearning criterion, which ensures that the unlearned model is, with high probability, close in parameter space to a model retrained from scratch. However, proximity in parameter space alone does not guarantee successful unlearning. While the two models may share similar characteristics, such as similar gradients or loss values, this does not imply that they encode identical knowledge, particularly on the unlearning data. More importantly, the ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -certification does not explicitly verify whether the unlearned model has actually forgotten the targeted data. It merely quantifies how indistinguishable the unlearned model is from a reference model under a distributional assumption. Thus, an unlearned model may still retain detailed information about the unlearning data while satisfying the certification criteria. As shown, models produced by Adversarial Retrain, Fine-tune, Relabel with Fine-tune, and Gradient Ascent with Fine-tune exhibit output distributions that closely resemble those of the retrained model, suggesting successful unlearning. In contrast, the Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian methods yield visualizations that are remarkably similar to the pre-unlearning model, indicating that the influence of the unlearning data has likely not been removed. Moreover, models produced by Relabeling and Gradient Ascent display highly scattered patterns, suggesting degraded utility and unstable behavior. These methods still exhibit high accuracy in classifying the unlearning data to their backdoored labels after unlearning, indicating that the corresponding models retain knowledge of the unlearning data. sections.heading: VII-B Robustness Study against Fake Unlearning
sections.text: To demonstrate the robustness of our auditing framework, we introduce an adversarial prover who attempts to bypass verification by replacing the true unlearning data with gradient-similar data. Specifically, the adversarial prover constructs a fake unlearning set D u ′ D_{u}^{\prime} by selecting samples from the remaining data D r D_{r} such that each sample in D u ′ D_{u}^{\prime} exhibits gradient-level similarity to a corresponding sample in the original unlearning set D u D_{u} . To construct D u ′ D_{u}^{\prime} , the adversarial prover first computes the gradient of the loss with respect to model parameters for each sample in D r D_{r} . Then, for each sample x x in D u D_{u} , the prover calculates its gradient and identifies the most similar sample x ′ x^{\prime} from D r D_{r} based on cosine similarity between their gradients. The selected x ′ x^{\prime} is then added to D u ′ D_{u}^{\prime} . To ensure uniqueness, if the most similar candidate has already been used, the prover selects the next most similar unused sample. This process is repeated iteratively until all samples in D u D_{u} are matched with distinct and gradient-similar counterparts from D r D_{r} . During unlearning, the adversarial prover unlearns the fake unlearning set D u ′ D_{u}^{\prime} instead of the true unlearning set D u D_{u} , aiming to retain the knowledge of D u D_{u} while evading our auditing. To give the adversary the best chance of success, we allow the use of the retraining-from-scratch approach, which has been shown to be the most likely to pass the verification based on the above results. We refer to this method as Fake Retraining . Another fake unlearning approach is from [ 7 ] . This method forges a plausible “proof of retraining” without actually performing full retraining on the remaining data D r D_{r} . If the current training data do not contain any unlearning samples, the model is updated using a single sample randomly selected from D r D_{r} . However, if the training data include unlearning samples, they are replaced with their nearest neighbors from D r D_{r} , and the model is updated using these substitutes. We refer to this method as Forging-based Retraining . The results are presented in Tables XIII , XIV , XV , XVI , XVII , and XVIII . sections.heading: VIII Extension to Large Language Models
sections.text: The proposed auditing method can also be extended to LLMs. Although a current trend in auditing LLM unlearning is to use adversarial auditing methods, such as membership inference, existing studies have shown that these approaches suffer from limited reliability [ 13 , 12 , 9 ] . Thus, our auditing framework can fill this gap. We consider a scenario where a pre-trained LLM, M M , is fine-tuned on a dataset D D , resulting in a fine-tuned model M ′ M^{\prime} . Now, suppose that a subset D u D_{u} of D D is requested to be unlearned, and the model provider applies an unlearning algorithm to remove D u D_{u} , producing an unlearned model M u ′ M^{\prime}_{u} . To audit whether the unlearning was successful, the model provider, acting as the prover, uses the original pre-trained LLM, M M , as the verification model. Since M M was never trained on D u D_{u} , it serves as a guaranteed verification model that excludes any information from D u D_{u} . The auditor then compares the outputs of M M and M u ′ M^{\prime}_{u} using the samples in D u D_{u} as input. If the outputs are consistent, the auditor concludes that M u ′ M^{\prime}_{u} does not retain information from D u D_{u} . Otherwise, the model provider is given another opportunity to refine the verification model. We follow the experimental setup in [ 38 ] to evaluate their proposed unlearning method. Their approach integrates key ideas from three unlearning methods: Gradient Ascent, Relabel (referred to as Random Mismatch in their work), and Fine-tuning (referred to as Maintain Performance). For the LLM, we adopt OPT-2.7B [ 39 ] . sections.heading: IX Related Work
sections.text: Machine Unlearning. Machine unlearning include two types: exact unlearning and approximate unlearning [ 6 ] . Exact unlearning typically involves retraining the model from scratch with the unlearned data removed from the training set. While this process can be optimized by partitioning the training set into multiple shards and retraining only on the shard containing the unlearned data [ 3 , 43 ] , it remains computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale models. In contrast, approximate unlearning seeks to modify the model’s parameters by applying updates over a limited number of epochs. The goal is to ensure that the modified model closely approximates the one obtained through full retraining in the parameter space [ 44 , 22 , 45 ] . Research on machine unlearning has recently expanded into the LLM domain [ 46 , 47 ] . While approximate unlearning remains an efficient approach [ 48 , 38 ] , a new form has emerged, focusing on controlling LLM outputs through prompt engineering [ 49 , 50 ] . Auditing Machine Unlearning. Machine unlearning can be intuitively audited by comparing the unlearned model to a reference model retrained from scratch either in parameter space or behavior space [ 6 , 8 ] . However, this approach assumes access to a freshly retrained model, which is often impractical due to the high computational cost. Alternative lines of work include certified unlearning [ 21 , 51 ] , which leverages differential privacy [ 52 ] to obscure the differences between the retrained and unlearned models, and reproducing verification [ 53 , 7 , 18 ] , which records the unlearning operations, enabling the data owner to reproduce each step and verify the integrity of the process. However, certified unlearning relies on the convexity of the loss function, limiting its applicability to more complex models. Although recent works [ 16 , 17 ] have extended certified unlearning to deep learning settings, these guarantees hold only when using their specific unlearning algorithms, and thus do not constitute a universal certification framework. Meanwhile, reproducing verification focuses on auditing the unlearning procedure rather than the unlearning outcomes. In the ML security domain, one intuitive approach to auditing unlearning is through membership inference attacks [ 54 ] . However, membership inference typically requires training a large number of shadow models, resulting in substantial computational overhead. Moreover, its inference accuracy remains insufficient for reliable verification in practical settings [ 11 , 9 ] . Another auditing strategy is backdoor-based verification, where data owners deliberately inject poisoned data into the training set to serve as backdoor triggers [ 15 ] . However, this method requires the injection of a sufficient amount of poisoned data into the training set prior to model training.

sections.heading: X Conclusion
sections.text: This paper has addressed a fundamental yet underexplored problem in machine unlearning: how to audit if unlearning has been successfully achieved. We propose the first universal auditing framework, inspired by the concept of proof of ignorance, that can effectively assess a wide range of unlearning methods across diverse datasets. Our framework applies not only to conventional ML models but also extends to LLMs. Future research will focus on extending this framework to support streaming unlearning under continual learning settings.

sections.heading: II Datasets and Unlearning Methods
sections.text: Datasets. • CIFAR10 [ 29 ] includes 60,000 60,000 images across 10 10 classes, each containing 6,000 6,000 images of vehicles and animals. The dimension of each image is 32 × 32 32\times 32 . • SVHN [ 30 ] is a street view house number dataset, consisting of 10 10 classes, each representing a digit. It comprises over 600,000 600,000 samples, each measuring 32 × 32 32\times 32 . • SkinCancer [ 31 ] is a melanoma skin cancer dataset containing 10,000 10,000 images, with 9,000 9,000 images for training and 1,000 1,000 for testing. The task is binary classification, and each image was resized to 32 × 32 32\times 32 . • BBCNews [ 32 ] consists of RSS Feeds from the BBC News site, comprising 29,500 29,500 records. Each record includes five attributes: title, pubDate, guid, link, and description. The dataset includes five classes: business, politics, entertainment, science, and sport. • AGNews [ 33 ] is a topic classification dataset composed of news articles categorized into four classes: World, Sports, Business, and Technology. Each class includes 30,000 30,000 training samples and 1,900 1,900 test samples. • IMDB [ 34 ] contains 50,000 movie reviews categorized for binary sentiment classification, distinguishing between positive and negative sentiments. The dataset comprises 25,000 highly polar movie reviews allocated for training and an additional 25,000 for testing purposes. Unlearning Methods. • Retrain. This method removes the unlearning data and retrains a new model on the remaining data. Variant includes SISA [ 3 ] , which trains models on data shards and retrains affected shards upon unlearning requests. • Adversarial retrain [ 7 ] . This method retrains a model from scratch without using unlearning samples. During retraining, each sample in the mini-batch is examined: if it belongs to the remaining data, it is retained for model updates; if it is an unlearning sample, the method selects a similar sample from the remaining data that produces a comparable gradient. • Fine-tuning (FT) [ 17 ] . This method directly fine-tunes the current model on the remaining data. Its variants [ 17 ] apply noisy fine-tuning on all or part of the remaining data. • Relabeling [ 22 ] . This family of methods modifies the unlearned data by assigning randomly selected incorrect labels, and uses the mislabeled data to fine-tune the model. • Relabeling with fine-tuning (Relabel+FT) [ 22 ] . This approach builds on the relabeling method. After unlearning, the unlearned model is further fine-tuned using the remaining data to improve its overall performance. • Gradient ascent (GA) [ 35 ] . This class of methods reverses the model’s training on the unlearned data by adding back the corresponding gradients. • Gradient ascent with fine-tuning (GA+FT) [ 35 ] . This approach fine-tunes the unlearned model on the remaining data after applying the gradient ascent unlearning method. • Fisher forgetting [ 36 ] . This method applies Gaussian noise to perturb the model towards exact unlearning. The Gaussian distribution has a zero mean and covariance determined by the 4 4 -th root of the Fisher information matrix with respect to the model on the unlearned data. • Hessian forgetting [ 36 , 37 ] . This method builds upon Fisher forgetting by replacing the Fisher Information Matrix with the Hessian matrix, which provides a second-order correction to achieve more precise unlearning. • Certified Hessian forgetting [ 16 ] . This method offers a theoretical guarantee of certified unlearning by modifying the model parameters using the inverse Hessian matrix of the loss function computed over the remaining data.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2606.16110v1 [cs.LG] 15 Jun 2026 Auditing Machine Unlearning: A Systematic Research on Whether Models Truly Forget Dayong Ye Tianqing Zhu * Ruiding Huang Xinbo Fu Jiayang Li Bo Liu Huan Huo Wanlei Zhou † † thanks: Tianqing Zhu is the corresponding author. Abstract Machine unlearning has been extensively studied in response to growing privacy concerns and regulatory requirements. However, auditing whether unlearning algorithms have truly erased the influence of specific data remains an open challenge. The lack of reliable and practical auditing mechanisms can lead to critical privacy risks, such as residual information leakage. This paper initiates a systematic investigation into whether existing unlearning algorithms can truly forget the designated data. We propose the first practical and general-purpose auditing framework for machine unlearning, inspired by the concept of proof of ignorance. Our framework addresses the key practicality limitations of existing methods by eliminating the need for retraining-from-scratch baselines, avoiding the training of large numbers of shadow models, and requiring no intrusive intervention in the original training process. To evaluate the effectiveness of our framework, we first conduct validation experiments to verify its soundness and completeness. We then perform comprehensive experiments across six datasets and ten representative unlearning methods. The results demonstrate that our framework reliably distinguishes between successful and failed unlearning. In particular, we observe that retraining-based and fine-tuning-based methods can achieve effective unlearning, even when the target data remain in the original dataset. In contrast, de-optimization-based methods fail to achieve true unlearning and instead degrade the model’s performance. Fisher/Hessian-based methods also fail to unlearn requested data, even formal certification is provided. Moreover, we show that our framework is robust against fake unlearning attempts and generalizes well to large language models. I Introduction Machine unlearning has emerged as a critical paradigm for enabling data deletion in machine learning models, particularly in response to growing concerns around user privacy and regulatory requirements such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [ 1 ] . The goal of unlearning is to ensure that a trained model forgets specific data samples upon request, such that the resulting model behaves as if the data had never been used in training [ 2 , 3 ] . Motivated by this objective, a wide range of unlearning algorithms has been proposed [ 4 , 5 ] . However, the problem of auditing unlearning outcomes remains largely underexplored. In most existing studies, outcome auditing is treated as a peripheral issue or mentioned only briefly, without a systematic investigation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Auditing machine unlearning is critical. Its goal is to determine whether the unlearned model has truly forgotten the knowledge associated with the data requested for removal. An effective audit not only reassures data owners who exercise their right to revoke personal data, but also certifies the correctness and reliability of unlearning algorithms. Straightforward auditing approaches include parametric auditing and behavioral auditing [ 6 , 8 ] . Parametric auditing evaluates whether the parameters of the unlearned model remain within a bounded distance from those of a model retrained from scratch without the unlearning data. In contrast, behavioral auditing assesses if the unlearned model exhibits similar behavior to that of the retrained model when evaluated on specific datasets. Despite their conceptual soundness, both approaches share a fundamental limitation: they require access to a retrained model that excludes the unlearning data. This renders them impractical for two reasons. First, retraining a model from scratch incurs substantial computational overhead. Second, if one already possesses the retrained model, auditing becomes unnecessary, as this retrained model can be directly deployed as the unlearned model. Another line of research on unlearning auditing is based on membership inference [ 9 , 10 ] , which aims to determine whether the unlearned data still belong to the training set of the unlearned model. However, membership inference typically requires training a large number of shadow models, resulting in heavy computational cost [ 11 ] . Moreover, it often suffers from limited inference accuracy and yields only probabilistic outcomes without explicit accuracy guarantees [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Other less mainstream auditing methods rely on backdoors, but they require the unrealistic step of injecting backdoors into the training data before model training [ 15 ] . An orthogonal research direction focuses on auditing unlearning procedures [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] , with the goal of verifying whether mutually agreed unlearning algorithms are executed correctly. In contrast, our work audits unlearning outcomes rather than procedures. This distinction is important because, as we show in the experiments, some unlearning algorithms fail to truly remove the influence of the unlearning data even if they are executed correctly. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a practical and general unlearning auditing framework by addressing three challenges . First , the absence of access to retrained reference models necessitates a self-contained auditing mechanism that does not rely on expensive retraining from scratch. Second , achieving a balance between auditing effectiveness and computational efficiency complicates the design: the auditing method must deliver reliable assessments while incurring significantly lower computational cost than full retraining. Third , there is no definitive ground truth for evaluating whether a given unlearning algorithm, apart from retraining from scratch, has truly achieved the unlearning objective. To address the first and second challenges, our auditing framework constructs verification models by training on only 15 % 15\% of the remaining data, on average, for each verification model. As our verification model is trained on data disjoint from the unlearning set, it provides a valid comparator for evaluating whether the unlearned model has successfully forgotten the targeted data, thus addressing the first challenge. This comparison is grounded in the concept of proof of ignorance. If a verification model, believed to lack knowledge of the unlearning set, can be transformed into the unlearned model through a polynomial-time process, such as updating it with additional data, then the unlearned model is also considered to be ignorant of the same knowledge. Thus, if the unlearned model exhibits behavior closely aligned with that of the verification model or its transformed version, it provides strong evidence that the unlearned model no longer retains the forgotten data. Moreover, although only a subset of the remaining data is used, our framework leverages the insight that a small but representative subset can still capture the distributional characteristics of the original data [ 19 ] , thus addressing the second challenge by striking a balance between computational efficiency and auditing accuracy. To address the third challenge, the lack of ground truth for successful unlearning, we first validate our framework before using it to audit unlearning methods. Then, we use backdoor-based and membership inference-based auditing, along with t-SNE [ 20 ] visualization, as supporting evidence. In summary, this paper makes three contributions . • We initiate a systematical study to examine whether existing popular unlearning algorithms can truly forget the revoked data. To achieve this, we propose the first practical and general auditing framework, grounded in the concept of proof of ignorance. Before applying the framework, we rigorously evaluate its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and validation experiments. • We perform a comprehensive empirical study that evaluates ten unlearning approaches across six datasets, including both image and text domains. We also assess our framework against fake unlearning attempts and demonstrate its effectiveness in successfully detecting them. • We further demonstrate the strong generalizability of our framework by extending the auditing study to large language model (LLM) unlearning scenarios. II Preliminary and Threat Model Machine Unlearning. Given a learning algorithm A : 𝒟 → ℳ A:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} , where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denotes the data space and ℳ \mathcal{M} represents the model space, a model M M can be trained using A A on a dataset D D , i.e., M = A ⁡ ( D ) M=A(D) . When an unlearning request is made to forget a subset of the data D u ⊂ D D_{u}\subset D , a straightforward approach is to retrain the model from scratch using A A on the remaining data D r = D − D u D_{r}=D-D_{u} , resulting in a perfectly unlearned model M u ∗ M^{*}_{u} , i.e., M u ∗ = A ⁡ ( D r ) M^{*}_{u}=A(D_{r}) . However, this retraining-from-scratch method is computationally intensive. Let U : ℳ × 𝒟 × 𝒟 → ℳ U:\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{D}\times\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} be an unlearning algorithm. An unlearned model M u M_{u} is obtained by applying U U to M M , D D , and D u D_{u} , i.e., M u = U ⁡ ( M , D , D u ) M_{u}=U(M,D,D_{u}) . Ideally, U U is more computationally efficient than retraining from scratch, and the difference between M u M_{u} and M u ∗ M^{*}_{u} is minimized. This difference can be quantified in either the model parameter space [ 21 , 22 ] or the model output space [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Proof of Ignorance. In the proof of ignorance [ 26 , 27 ] , given an instance q q of a complex problem, the prover must demonstrate to the auditor that they do not know the solution s s for the problem q q . To address this, the prover identifies a well-known complex instance q ′ q^{\prime} , with a solution s ′ s^{\prime} that is computationally related to s s , namely, there exists a polynomial-time process that transforms s ′ s^{\prime} to s s . As q ′ q^{\prime} is both well-known and complex, claiming ignorance of its solution s ′ s^{\prime} is considered trustworthy by the auditor. Moreover, since s ′ s^{\prime} is computationally related to s s , ignorance of s ′ s^{\prime} implies ignorance of s s . Threat Model. The model provider employs an unlearning algorithm U U to remove the influence of the requested data D u D_{u} , as specified by the data owner, resulting in an unlearned model M u M_{u} . The model provider, acting as the prover , then aims to validate that the unlearned model M u M_{u} no longer contains information related to D u D_{u} . This validation can be presented either to the data owner or to a trusted third party, such as a regulator, who acts as the auditor . The prover has full access to the original model M M and the training data D D , and can freely modify M M or utilize D D as needed. In contrast, the auditor does not have access to the internal parameters of M M or its variants but can query these models and observe their outputs. The auditor holds the authority to define and enforce the auditing protocol. In particular, the auditor can specify which portions of the data D D are used during the auditing process without accessing the actual data content, and the prover follows these auditing instructions throughout the protocol. This assumption is reasonable, as our objective is to audit the efficacy of unlearning algorithms rather than the honesty of the prover. We will relax this assumption in the experiments by considering scenarios in which the prover performs fake unlearning. This asymmetry of access reflects real-world scenarios where the model provider (the prover) is an ML service platform, while the auditor is a data owner or regulatory authority with limited insight into the internal workings of the model. The assumption that the auditor cannot see the raw data in D D , but can still reference its structure (e.g., via hashes), is reasonable. It reflects the common setting in privacy-preserving audits [ 28 ] , where the auditor must operate under a black-box model due to data sensitivity. Problem Statement. Given an unlearned model M u M_{u} , the original model M M , the unlearning data D u D_{u} , and the original training data D D , our goal is to design an auditing framework 𝒱 \mathcal{V} that produces a binary outcome indicating whether M u M_{u} has successfully forgotten D u D_{u} . Specifically, 𝒱 ⁡ ( M u , M , D u , D ) → { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{V}(M_{u},M,D_{u},D)\rightarrow\{0,1\} , where “ 1 1 ” denotes successful unlearning and “ 0 0 ” indicates failure. The notations used in this paper are shown in Table I . TABLE I: Summary of Notations Notations Description M M The pre-unlearning original model D D The data used to train M M D u ⊂ D D_{u}\subset D The data requested to be unlearned from M M D r D_{r} The remaining data, where D r ∪ D u = D D_{r}\cup D_{u}=D D t D_{t} The test data, where D t ∩ D = ∅ D_{t}\cap D=\emptyset M u M_{u} The unlearned model claimed to have forgotten D u D_{u} D v ⊂ D r D_{v}\subset D_{r} The data used for verification M v M_{v} The verification model trained by D v D_{v} III Methodology Rationale. According to the proof of ignorance, the prover can generate another model M v M_{v} that is guaranteed to exclude the data D u D_{u} . If the prover can then demonstrate that M v M_{v} can be transformed into M u M_{u} through a polynomial-time process, such as further updating M v M_{v} with additional data from D r D_{r} , it becomes credible to assert that M u M_{u} does not contain information from D u D_{u} . Detailed theoretical analyses of our auditing framework are provided in Section IV . Fig. 1: Overview of our auditing framework. The auditor first conducts a preliminary check by comparing outputs from the unlearned model M u M_{u} and the pre-unlearning model M M . If their behavior is highly consistent, unlearning is immediately considered failed. Otherwise, the auditor proceeds to the main protocol: Step 1, the prover trains a verification model M v M_{v} ; Step 2, the auditor compares outputs between M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} ; Step 3, if inconsistent, M v M_{v} is updated or retrained and compared again. If consistency is achieved, unlearning is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected. Overview. As shown in Figure 1 , before initiating the formal auditing process, we conduct a preliminary check: if the unlearned model exhibits behavior nearly identical to the pre-unlearning model, for example, both achieving high accuracy on the unlearning set, it can be immediately flagged as a failure of unlearning. This is because a truly unlearned model is expected to undergo a noticeable behavioral shift, particularly in its performance on the unlearning data. Once such obvious failures are filtered out, we proceed with the main auditing protocol, which consists of three steps . First , the auditor randomly identifies a subset of data D v D_{v} from the remaining data D r = D − D u D_{r}=D-D_{u} , and instructs the prover to use D v D_{v} as a verification set to train a new model M v M_{v} for auditing. Since D v D_{v} is entirely disjoint from D u D_{u} , it is guaranteed that M v M_{v} does not contain any information from D u D_{u} . Second , the auditor compares the outputs of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} . If the outputs of the two models are consistent, it can be trusted that M u M_{u} also does not contain the information of D u D_{u} . This is because consistent outputs indicate that M u M_{u} and M v M_{v} exhibit similar decision boundaries on D u D_{u} . As M v M_{v} is independent of D u D_{u} , such consistence implies that M u M_{u} ’s behavior does not rely on specific features derived from D u D_{u} . However, if the outputs of the two models are inconsistent, the audit proceeds to the third step. In the third step, based on the observed differences in outputs between M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} , the prover decides whether to increase the size of D v D_{v} by adding more data from D r D_{r} or to reduce the size of D v D_{v} by removing some data. If the decision is to increase the size of D v D_{v} , the prover fine-tunes M v M_{v} using the additional data. If the decision is to reduce the size of D v D_{v} , the prover retrains M v M_{v} using the reduced subset. After refining M v M_{v} , the auditor compares the outputs of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} again. If the outputs are consistent, the prover can claim that M u M_{u} does not contain the information of D u D_{u} . If the outputs remain inconsistent, the prover fails to prove ignorance of the presence of D u D_{u} in M u M_{u} . The auditor grants the prover only a single opportunity to refine M v M_{v} for auditing. We will show in Section IV that this single refinement is sufficient to ensure correctness. Each step of our method is elaborated in detail. Step 1. Verification Model Construction. The auditor randomly selects a subset of data from D r D_{r} to form a new dataset D v D_{v} . This selection can be implemented using various randomized sampling techniques to ensure that D v D_{v} is representative of the overall distribution of D r D_{r} while remaining entirely disjoint from D u D_{u} . One straightforward approach is uniform random sampling, where each data point in D r D_{r} has an equal probability of being included in D v D_{v} . This method ensures that the selection process is unbiased and does not favor any particular subset of data. Alternatively, the auditor can use stratified random sampling, where the data points are grouped based on their class labels. Samples are then drawn randomly from each group in proportion to their representation in D r D_{r} . This technique ensures that D v D_{v} retains a distribution similar to that of D r D_{r} , making the auditing process more robust against imbalances in the dataset. Both approaches will be evaluated. For the size of D v D_{v} , a common heuristic is to define it as a fraction of the size of D r D_{r} , i.e., | D v | = α ⋅ | D r | |D_{v}|=\alpha\cdot|D_{r}| , where α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in(0,1] . A larger α \alpha ensures that D v D_{v} is more representative of D r D_{r} , while a smaller α \alpha reduces computational overhead. We treat α \alpha as a hyperparameter that can be tuned based on auditing accuracy requirements. After forming D v D_{v} , the prover uses it to train a verification model M v M_{v} . As D v D_{v} is disjoint from D u D_{u} , it is guaranteed that M v M_{v} does not incorporate any information related to D u D_{u} . This property makes M v M_{v} a clean reference model for auditing the unlearning process. Step 2. Output Comparison for Auditing. After training the verification model M v M_{v} , the auditor compares its outputs with those of the unlearned model M u M_{u} using the unlearning set D u D_{u} . For each sample x ∈ D u x\in D_{u} , the auditor checks if M v ​ ( x ) = M u ​ ( x ) M_{v}(x)=M_{u}(x) and computes an auditing metric υ \upsilon , defined as: υ = ∑ x ∈ D u 𝟙 [ M v ( x ) = M u ( x ) ] | D u | , \upsilon=\frac{\sum_{x\in D_{u}}\mathds{1}[M_{v}(x)=M_{u}(x)]}{|D_{u}|}, (1) where 𝟙 M v ​ ( x ) = M u ​ ( x ) \mathds{1}_{M_{v}(x)=M_{u}(x)} is an indicator function that equals 1 1 if the outputs of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} are identical for a given x x , and 0 0 otherwise. The metric υ \upsilon represents the proportion of data samples in D u D_{u} for which the two models produce consistent outputs. Ideally, υ \upsilon should equal 1 1 to provide absolute certainty in the audit. However, achieving υ = 1 \upsilon=1 is challenging due to the arbitrary initialization and inherent variability in model training. To address this, we adopt a pre-defined threshold ζ \zeta , treated as a hyperparameter. If υ \upsilon exceeds the threshold ζ \zeta , it is trusted that M u M_{u} does not contain information from D u D_{u} . Otherwise, the audit proceeds to the third step. The threshold ζ \zeta determines the acceptable level of consistency. It should be based on the expected agreement between two independent models trained on disjoint datasets unrelated to D u D_{u} . This is captured by the baseline agreement rate υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e \upsilon_{base} , estimated as: υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e = ∑ x ∈ D u 𝟙 [ M v 1 ( x ) = M v 2 ( x ) ] | D u | , \upsilon_{base}=\frac{\sum_{x\in D_{u}}\mathds{1}[M_{v_{1}}(x)=M_{v_{2}}(x)]}{|D_{u}|}, (2) where M v 1 M_{v_{1}} and M v 2 M_{v_{2}} are independent models trained on disjoint subsets of D r D_{r} . After obtaining υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e \upsilon_{base} , ζ \zeta can be set by adding a safety margin to υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e \upsilon_{base} to account for variability in training and noise in υ \upsilon . Specifically, ζ \zeta is defined as: ζ = υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e + k ⋅ σ , \zeta=\upsilon_{base}+k\cdot\sigma, (3) where σ = υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e ​ ( 1 − υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e ) | D u | \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\upsilon_{base}(1-\upsilon_{base})}{|D_{u}|}} is the approximate standard error of υ \upsilon , and k k is a confidence multiplier, e.g., k = 2 k=2 for 95 % 95\% confidence. The actual standard error of υ \upsilon is: σ = p ⁡ ( 1 − p ) | D u | \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{|D_{u}|}} , where p p is the true probability of agreement for a single sample x ∈ D u x\in D_{u} between M v ​ ( x ) M_{v}(x) and M u ​ ( x ) M_{u}(x) , as υ \upsilon follows the distribution: υ ∼ Binomial ⁡ ( | D u | , p ) | D u | \upsilon\sim\frac{{\rm Binomial}(|D_{u}|,p)}{|D_{u}|} . However, since p p is unknown, we approximate it using υ b ​ a ​ s ​ e \upsilon_{base} . Step 3. Verification Model Refinement. When υ < ζ \upsilon<\zeta , the unlearned model M u M_{u} cannot be trusted to have completely forgotten D u D_{u} . Given the inherent randomness in model training, the prover is allowed another opportunity to refine their verification model M v M_{v} . This refinement is guided by the accuracy difference between M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} on the unlearning data D u D_{u} . Formally, let A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) Acc(M_{v},D_{u}) and A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) Acc(M_{u},D_{u}) be the accuracy of M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} , respectively, on D u D_{u} . Comparing their accuracy can lead to three possible outcomes. First, if A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) < A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) Acc(M_{v},D_{u})<Acc(M_{u},D_{u}) , this suggests one of two possibilities: (1) the generalizability of M v M_{v} is worse than M u M_{u} , or (2) M u M_{u} retains information from D u D_{u} . The auditor then increases the size of the verification set D v D_{v} by sampling additional data from D r D_{r} to improve the generalizability of M v M_{v} . The exact number of additional data points can be determined based on the accuracy difference between A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) Acc(M_{v},D_{u}) and A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) Acc(M_{u},D_{u}) , denoted as Δ a ​ c ​ c = A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) − A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) \Delta_{acc}=Acc(M_{u},D_{u})-Acc(M_{v},D_{u}) . The size of the additional data to be added can be computed as: β ​ Δ a ​ c ​ c ​ | D r | \beta\Delta_{acc}|D_{r}| , where β ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \beta\in(0,1) is a scaling coefficient. This formulation aims to enhance the generalizability of M v M_{v} in a targeted manner, allowing M v M_{v} to better approximate M u M_{u} without over-correcting. Note that although the amount of additional data is computed linearly with respect to the accuracy gap Δ a ​ c ​ c \Delta_{acc} and the size of D r D_{r} , this does not imply a linear relationship between model accuracy and dataset size. Rather, the computation is used only to determine a sufficient amount of data for aligning the behavior of M v M_{v} with that of M u M_{u} . A formal analysis of this formulation is provided in Corollary 1 . After fine-tuning M v M_{v} with the expanded D v D_{v} , the auditor re-evaluates its consistency with M u M_{u} . If M v M_{v} and M u M_{u} remain inconsistent, the auditor can conclude that M u M_{u} contains information from D u D_{u} . Second, if A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) > A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) Acc(M_{v},D_{u})>Acc(M_{u},D_{u}) , this suggests that the unlearned model M u M_{u} may be either over-unlearned or severely degraded, depending on the magnitude of the accuracy difference Δ a ​ c ​ c = A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M v , D u ) − A ​ c ​ c ​ ( M u , D u ) \Delta_{acc}=Acc(M_{v},D_{u})-Acc(M_{u},D_{u}) . To address this, the verifier reduces the size of the verification set D v D_{v} by removing a portion of its data and retrains M v M_{v} on the reduced D v D_{v} . The number of data points to remove is determined as β ​ Δ a ​ c ​ c ​ | D r | \beta\Delta_{acc}|D_{r}| . This adjustment intentionally reduces the performance of M v M_{v} to align more closely with the over-unlearned or degraded behavior of M u M_{u} . After retraining M v M_{v} on the reduced D v D_{v} , the auditor re-evaluates its consistency with M u M_{u} . If the two models remain inconsistent, the auditor concludes that M u M_{u} retains information from D u D_{u} . V Experimental Setup Datasets and Model Architectures. We use three image datasets: CIFAR10 [ 29 ] , SVHN [ 30 ] , and SkinCancer [ 31 ] , and three text datasets: BBCNews [ 32 ] , AGNews [ 33 ] , and IMDB [ 34 ] , covering both multi-class and binary classification tasks, to evaluate the multi-modal applicability of the proposed auditing framework. For image datasets, the model architecture consists of four CNN blocks followed by three fully connected layers. For text datasets, the model includes an embedding layer, three CNN blocks, and a fully connected layer. Unlearning Methods. We evaluate four representative unlearning methods, along with six of their variants, including Retrain , Adversarial retrain [ 7 ] , Fine-tuning (FT) [ 17 ] , Relabeling [ 22 ] , Relabeling with fine-tuning (Relabel+FT) [ 22 ] , Gradient ascent (GA) [ 35 ] , Gradient ascent with fine-tuning (GA+FT) [ 35 ] , Fisher forgetting [ 36 ] , Hessian forgetting [ 36 , 37 ] , and Certified Hessian forgetting [ 16 ] . Detailed descriptions of these unlearning approaches and datasets are provided in the Appendix. Evaluation Metrics. Since our auditing method relies primarily on model outputs, the evaluation metrics are centered around comparing the outputs of different models. • Model agreement. This metric, defined in Eq. 1 , quantifies the consistency between the outputs of two models. It is calculated as the ratio of the number of data points for which both models produce identical outputs to the total number of data points in the given dataset. This metric is widely used in the literature to evaluate model similarity. • Average Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL). This metric complements the model agreement by measuring the average KL divergence between the output probability distributions of two models across a given dataset. Baselines. We adopt widely recognized auditing methods as baselines [ 4 , 7 ] . • Model Accuracy on the Unlearning Data. This is a straightforward auditing method. The intuition is that if the unlearning data have been properly forgotten, the unlearned model should perform on them similarly to how it performs on the test data. • Membership Inference. This method determines whether a given data sample was in the training set of a target model. If the model has truly forgotten the unlearning data, a membership inference attack should identify them as non-training data. We employ the state of the art technique proposed in [ 9 ] . • Backdoor-based Auditing. This method leverages the principle behind backdoor attacks, where specific data are intentionally misclassified into targeted labels. When the unlearning data are backdoored, a successful unlearning process should eliminate their influence, meaning that the model should no longer misclassify these samples into the targeted labels. For a fair comparison, we adopt the same backdoor attack method used in [ 7 ] . Following the three-step main auditing protocol, the final agreement rates between the unlearned model M u M_{u} and the verification model M v M_{v} for these methods all exceed the base agreement threshold of 70.30 70.30 . Specifically, the agreement rates are 71.23 71.23 for Retrain, 71.10 71.10 for Adversarial Retrain, 70.53 70.53 for Fine-tune, 70.94 70.94 for Relabel with Fine-tune, and 70.33 70.33 for Gradient Ascent with Fine-tune. Therefore, these methods are deemed to have achieved successful unlearning. This auditing outcome can be further attributed to the nature of these methods. By either retraining the model from scratch or performing targeted fine-tuning on the remaining data, they effectively eliminate the influence of the unlearning data. Thus, the decision boundaries of the unlearned models align closely with those of the verification model. We pay particular attention to the Fine-tune approach, which directly fine-tunes the model on the remaining data without explicitly interacting with or removing the unlearning data. At first glance, this method may appear inadequate from an algorithmic standpoint, as it continues training a model that initially retains knowledge of the unlearning data. However, our auditing results suggest that this approach can indeed achieve the unlearning objective. The underlying reason lies in the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, where continued training on new data causes a model to lose previously acquired knowledge. By exclusively fine-tuning on the remaining data, this forgetting effect is concentrated on the unlearning data, erasing its influence from the model. Another approach that warrants close attention is Adversarial Retrain. Although this method is described as “adversarial” in [ 7 ] , our auditing results suggest that it effectively achieves the unlearning objective. The key mechanism is that it intentionally avoids using the unlearning data during retraining. Instead, it replaces each unlearning sample with a feature-similar sample selected from the remaining dataset. We argue that this substitution strategy constitutes a valid unlearning mechanism. First, it strictly adheres to the unlearning requirement, as the actual unlearning data are excluded from the retraining process. Second, the use of feature-similar data does not violate the privacy or intent of data revocation. These substitute samples are drawn from the remaining, non-revoked data, and therefore do not reintroduce any personal information that the data owner has requested to remove. These methods attempt to “unlearn” by deliberately corrupting the model’s performance on the unlearning data, typically through perturbing the decision boundaries or reversing the gradients associated with those samples. The fundamental flaw in these approaches is their reliance on performance deterioration as a proxy for forgetting. However, poor performance on the unlearning data does not guarantee that the model no longer retains knowledge of those data. In fact, a well-generalized model can perform well even on unseen data that shares the same distribution. Our auditing results support this argument. The models produced by these de-optimization-based approaches exhibit low agreement with verification models. For instance, in Table V , the agreement rates for Relabel and Gradient Ascent are only 30.90 30.90 and 35.17 35.17 , respectively, substantially below the base agreement threshold of 70.30 70.30 . The Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian Forgetting methods also fail to achieve the true objective of unlearning. Fisher Forgetting and Certified Hessian Forgetting can be rejected at an early stage by the preliminary check, as the resulting unlearned models exhibit behavior that is nearly indistinguishable from that of the pre-unlearning model. For instance, in Table V , the accuracy of the Fisher-based unlearned model on the unlearning set D u D_{u} , the remaining set D r D_{r} , and the test set D t D_{t} is 95.87 95.87 , 95.45 95.45 , and 71.62 71.62 , respectively, closely matching the pre-unlearning model’s accuracy of 95.92 95.92 , 95.61 95.61 , and 71.79 71.79 . In contrast, Hessian Forgetting can be readily filtered out by the preliminary check on the image datasets (Tables V , VI , and VII ), but it passes the preliminary check on the text datasets (Tables VIII , IX , and X ) as its accuracy on the unlearning data is substantially reduced. However, this reduction in accuracy is accompanied by a similarly significant drop in agreement with the verification model, and it is therefore still easily identified as a failed unlearning method by the subsequent auditing steps. The underlying reason lies in the design of these approaches. They attempt to remove the influence of the unlearning data through local parameter perturbations derived from second-order approximations of the loss landscape, such as the Fisher information matrix or the Hessian matrix. However, such perturbations are often too limited to induce the behavioral shift required for true unlearning. In some cases, they merely preserve the original model behavior, causing the resulting model to remain highly similar to the pre-unlearning model. In other cases, they degrade model accuracy without genuinely removing the influence of the unlearning data. We pay particular attention to the Certified Hessian unlearning method, as it fails to achieve effective unlearning despite being formally certified. Specifically, the certification refers to satisfying the ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -unlearning criterion, which ensures that the unlearned model is, with high probability, close in parameter space to a model retrained from scratch. However, proximity in parameter space alone does not guarantee successful unlearning. While the two models may share similar characteristics, such as similar gradients or loss values, this does not imply that they encode identical knowledge, particularly on the unlearning data. More importantly, the ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -certification does not explicitly verify whether the unlearned model has actually forgotten the targeted data. It merely quantifies how indistinguishable the unlearned model is from a reference model under a distributional assumption. Thus, an unlearned model may still retain detailed information about the unlearning data while satisfying the certification criteria. The results are presented in Tables XI , where accuracy on D u D_{u} denotes the proportion of samples correctly classified as backdoored labels. These results serve as strong empirical support for the conclusions drawn from our auditing method. In this setting, we apply a backdoor to all unlearning data, such that before unlearning, these data points are highly likely to be classified into their backdoored labels. After unlearning, a successful unlearning process should remove the influence of these poisoned associations, restoring the classification of unlearning data to their original, non-backdoored labels. Consistent with this intuition, the results show that before unlearning, all the unlearning data are reliably classified into the backdoored labels across datasets. After unlearning, five methods: Retrain, Adversarial Retrain, Fine-tuning, Relabeling with Fine-tuning, and Gradient Ascent with Fine-tuning achieve extremely low accuracy on the backdoored labels for the unlearning data, while maintaining high accuracy on the remaining data and the test set. This strongly aligns with our conclusion: these fine-tuning-based methods are effective at forgetting the unlearning data. In contrast, Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian Forgetting fail to erase the backdoor information. These methods still exhibit high accuracy in classifying the unlearning data to their backdoored labels after unlearning, indicating that the corresponding models retain knowledge of the unlearning data. For the Relabel and Gradient Ascent methods, although they reduce accuracy on backdoored labels after unlearning, they also significantly degrade performance on the remaining and test data. This suggests that the observed reduction in backdoor accuracy is not due to successful unlearning, but rather a side effect of harming overall model utility. Membership inference-based method does not yield reliable results due to a high false positive rate, as shown in Tables XII . For example, after unlearning via the Retrain method, all unlearning data should ideally be inferred as non-members. Yet, in practice, most of them are still identified as members, indicating the method’s limited precision. However, comparing the membership inference results across different unlearning methods still provides useful insights. The proportion of unlearning data that are incorrectly inferred as members is significantly higher for the Relabel, Gradient Ascent, Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian methods than for Retrain. This suggests that models unlearned using these methods retain more residual information about the unlearning data than retrained models. In other words, these methods fail to fully forget the unlearning data. Summary. Our auditing framework shows that retraining and fine-tuning-based approaches can successfully remove the influence of the unlearning data. In contrast, the Fisher, Hessian, and Certified Hessian methods consistently fail to achieve effective unlearning. The de-optimization-based approaches, Relabel and Gradient Ascent, merely degrade model performance without truly forgetting the targeted knowledge.
